newsitem.title: INDIA: India power struggle in bungalow drawing rooms.
newsitem.headline: India power struggle in bungalow drawing rooms.

text.p: A power struggle is being played out in the parlours of India's capital as Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda and his main rival jockey for advantage, but analysts said on Monday the prime minister is safe for now.

The scene of the tussle has been bungalow drawing rooms, not the corridors of power, as Deve Gowda and Congress party president Sitaram Kesri send signals of mounting displeasure by snubbing each other's social invitations.
Last week Deve Gowda pointedly failed to attend a reception hosted by Kesri reception to mark the breaking of the daily fast during the Moslem month of Ramadan.
The next day's newspapers were plastered with articles saying Deve Gowda's absence reflected growing ill will between the leaders.

In a tit-for-tat gesture, Kesri, who took over leadership of Congress in September after the party suffered its worst ever showing in general elections, boycotted Deve Gowda's own "iftar" reception on Saturday evening.
"Games at the Centre", wrote columnist Kuldip Nayar in The Hindustan Times.
Few doubted that Kesri would eventually challenge the prime minister for control of a badly fractured parliament.
Deve Gowda was thrust to the head of the government last June after the Communist Party of India-Marxist denied its leader, Jyoti Basu, the chance to take over the reins.
Kesri heads the second largest party in parliament, controlling 140 votes in the 545-seat lower house and a crucial say in whether the coalition survives.
The Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), which held power for 12 days in May before resigning in the face of certain defeat in a test vote, has 161 seats.

A former apostle of Mahatma Gandhi, Kesri has spearheaded a reunification drive by Congress, which suffered a rash of defections during the election campaign by leaders disenchanted with former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao.

Kesri has managed to push Rao, charged in three separate criminal corruption cases, to the sidelines and brought several disaffected leaders back into the fold. Rao denies any wrongdoing in the cases.

The new Congress chief was questioned earlier this month by the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI), the federal police agency, in connection with public interest litigation accusing Kesri of amassing wealth disproportionate to his known income.

The interrogation sent a chill through the Congress camp, which interpreted the move as a signal from Deve Gowda to Kesri to keep his distance. But the prime minister said he had no control over the CBI's work.
Kesri, meanwhile, has quietly held talks with leaders of Deve Gowda's coalition partners, newspapers said.

Analysts said the manoeuvring reflected increased tension between the two men but discounted the possibility that Congress would soon pull the rug out from under the United Front government, which controls about 190 seats in parliament.

"I don't think Congress is at all keen to precipitate a crisis that would mean going back to elections which they don't want because they would do badly," said Ashis Nandy of the Centre for the Study of Developing Societies.
"There is no immediate danger to Mr Deve Gowda," columnist Nayar wrote.

Pran Chopra of the Centre for Policy Research said Kesri had not yet managed to draw back Congress rebels, including Finance Minister P. Chidambaram, whose Tamil Manila Congress won 20 key seats in the southern state of Tamil Nadu last year.
Nandy said Congress would eventually try to displace Deve Gowda's socialist Janata Dal at the centre of an anti-BJP coalition without provoking fresh polls.
"I don't think there will be an immediate crisis as Kesri is new and has not consolidated his position," Nandy said. "Perhaps next year."
